#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when you want one place to decide every version*
This scenario demonstrates how to use a Bill of Materials (BOM), imported into `<dependencyManagement>`, to centralise version decisions.

This decouples "what I need" from "which version I need".

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] -- imports --> BOM[demo-bom:1.0.0]
    Root --> LibA[lib-a:?]
    Root --> LibB[lib-b:?]
    BOM -. defines .-> LibA_Ver[lib-a:1.0.0]
    BOM -. defines .-> LibB_Ver[lib-b:1.0.0]
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s3-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Importing a BOM centralises version control: direct dependencies declared without a version get the BOM's version, and transitive dependencies are held to it too.

#### ! Why
`<dependencyManagement>` supplies a default version for any dependency declared without one, and it also overrides the version of any *transitive* dependency it names, wherever that dependency appears in the graph. A BOM is just a POM whose `<dependencyManagement>` section you import with `<scope>import</scope>`, so one file can carry a whole set of versions that were tested together.

#### ! Fix
*   **Import the BOM** in `<dependencyManagement>` with `<type>pom</type>` and `<scope>import</scope>`.
*   **Delete the `<version>`** from every direct dependency the BOM manages. A version you leave behind overrides the BOM ([MS4](../scenario-4-override/guide.qmd)).
*   **Confirm with `mvn help:effective-pom`** that the managed versions are present.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Importing a vendor BOM (Spring Boot, Jakarta EE) that was tested as a set.
* MEDIUM Importing two BOMs that manage the same artifact. The first import wins, silently.
* HIGH Writing your own BOM and never updating it. A stale managed version downgrades every transitive that asks for something newer ([MS12](../scenario-12-metadata/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Control
This *is* the safer way. Prefer BOMs or a parent POM's `<dependencyManagement>` over version numbers scattered across modules.

#### ! Check

```bash
mvn help:effective-pom
```

**What to look for:**
The `<dependencyManagement>` section of the output. It should contain the versions defined in your BOM.

**Conclusion:**
If the versions are present, the BOM is correctly imported and influencing the build.

#### ! Scales
Essential for multi-module projects and microservices to ensure all services use the same library versions.

#### ! Takeaway
Centralised dependency management is the single most effective tool for preventing dependency drift.

#### ! Wild
The [Spring Boot BOM](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/appendix/dependency-versions/index.html) manages several hundred artifacts, and most Boot projects never write a version number for any of them. When a project inherits from `spring-boot-starter-parent` or imports `spring-boot-dependencies`, a single `<version>` on the parent decides Jackson, Hibernate, Tomcat and Micrometer at once. That is the pattern this scenario shows in miniature, and it is why a Boot upgrade is one line in the POM and a long afternoon of testing.
